newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia-NATO talks fail to resolve differences.
newsitem.headline: Russia-NATO talks fail to resolve differences.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov met for five hours on Monday but failed to resolve differences over the Western alliance's enlargement plans.

Their meeting, shrouded in secrecy at an official residence outside Moscow, produced agreement only on a schedule for more talks and on the fact that negotiations between the two former Cold War foes will not be easy over the next few months.
"The meeting was useful although, of course, there are different approaches on a range of questions," a brief Russian foreign ministry statement said.
"Discussions will be continued. A timetable has been set for future work. It is clear that it will not be easy but the two sides will try to make them a success."
A statement issued at NATO headquarters in Brussels was almost identical.

Relations are overshadowed by disagreement over NATO's plans to take in former Soviet bloc countries from eastern and central Europe. Moscow says such expansion would threaten its security and cause new divisions in Europe.
Little time remains for reaching an understanding before a July summit in Madrid at which NATO is expected to issue invitations to the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland.
Solana was expected to address Moscow's concerns by discussing terms for a special relationship with Russia and holding out the prospect of setting up a permanent mechanism for joint consultations.
Both sides played down the likelihood of a major breakthrough before the talks and made clear the path to agreement would be long and difficult.
"It is just the first round...in mutual relations between Russia and NATO," Sergei Yastrzhembsky, President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary, told a Kremlin briefing.
"I wouldn't have raised expectations about this meeting between Solana and Primakov," he said.

The chances of breaking the impasse appeared particularly low without the presence of Yeltsin, 65, who left hospital on Monday after 12 days of treatment for pneumonia. Yeltsin dominates foreign policy and all major decisions depend on him.

Yeltsin, his grip on power already in question because of his health problems, will be open to fierce criticism by his political rivals if he fails to win concessions before NATO expansion goes ahead.
Yastrzhembsky made clear Moscow would not accept vague promises from NATO.
"Russia and NATO must move to specific, hard and concrete discussions. Moscow doesn't believe in vague declarations and eloquent promises...which are not written down," he said.
"The period of romanticism in diplomacy is over," he said in reference to a honeymoon period in relations with the West as the Soviet Union collapsed.

The Kremlin turned its attention firmly back to foreign policy after Yeltsin ended almost six months out of his Kremlin office with health problems on December 23, two months after he had heart surgery.
He has ordered the foreign ministry to start drawing up a set of possible responses to an enlarged NATO.
Western diplomats say Russia appears intent on delaying enlargement, limiting the number of countries that join NATO and seeking as many concessions as possible.
